I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette:
Kofi is a 19-year-old Ghanaian-American UX designer who presents for an initial psychological evaluation following a period of sustained stalking that began approximately eight months ago. He is single, lives alone in a studio apartment, and works remotely for a small tech startup - a living arrangement that, in the months since the stalking began, has come to feel less like independence and less like safety than it once did.

The stalking was carried out by a former classmate from Kofi's design program, someone he had known casually and had been friendly toward over the course of a semester. Kofi had shared his portfolio online, engaged in the way young professionals are encouraged to do - commenting on work, responding to messages, being open and collegial. When the classmate's attention shifted from professional admiration to something more consuming, Kofi did not immediately recognise it. By the time he did, the person had begun appearing outside his building, sending repeated messages across multiple platforms, and on one occasion following him for several blocks after he left a coffee shop where he often worked. The incident at the coffee shop was the one that lodged most deeply. Kofi had been sitting at his usual table near the window - laptop open, headphones in - when he noticed the figure outside. He left quickly, and the figure followed. He did not feel safe until he had locked his apartment door behind him and sat on the floor with his back against it, heart hammering.

In the months that followed, Kofi has come to understand the world in a way that feels both inescapable and exhausting. He has come to believe, with a quiet but persistent certainty, that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place - that the openness he once moved through it with was naïve, perhaps even reckless. What troubles him most is a conviction he cannot fully shake: that he brought this on himself. He replays the semester in his mind - the comments he made, the messages he answered, the warmth he extended - and concludes that he acted in ways that invited what happened. He knows, in some abstract sense, that this reasoning is flawed, but the feeling of culpability sits in him like a stone. If he had been less friendly, less visible, less himself, perhaps none of it would have followed him home.

This belief has reorganised how he moves through his days. Working remotely as a UX designer means Kofi spends long hours at his desk, and the same digital fluency that defines his profession now carries a constant undercurrent of threat. He monitors his professional profiles with a vigilance that has little to do with career management - scanning for unfamiliar names, checking who has viewed his work, hesitating before posting anything that might signal his location or routine. He has removed his neighbourhood from his bio, turned off read receipts, and stopped updating the portfolio page that once made him proud. The coffee shop where he used to work most productively - the one near the window - he has not returned to. He now works exclusively from his apartment, and though the isolation is wearing on him, he tells himself this is simply what careful people do.

He is careful about everything now. He checks the street before leaving his building, varies his routes on the rare occasions he goes out, and finds himself scanning faces in a way that never used to be his habit. He is certain that you can never truly know what someone is capable of, that threat can emerge from ordinary friendliness, and that the only reasonable response is sustained alertness.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a project review at work. His supervisor noted, gently but clearly, that his output had slowed and that he had become difficult to reach. Kofi sat with that feedback for two weeks before booking an appointment. He is not sure what he is hoping for, exactly - he does not expect to feel safe again in the way he once did. What he wants, more than anything, is to stop feeling responsible for what happened to him.
